PHYSICAL ABILITY / AGILITY PRE-EMPLOYMENT TESTING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California and federal law governing when Acme, Inc. may require a job applicant for the position of Software Engineer, such as Acme, Inc., to complete a physical or agility test before or after a conditional job offer, and the legal framework that applies when such a test screens out applicants at different rates based on a protected characteristic. It states facts about what the Fair Employment and Housing Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and their implementing regulations permit, require, and restrict in this area. It is not itself a physical or agility test, a job description, or a validation study, and it does not tell Acme, Inc. or Acme, Inc. what to do about any particular hiring decision. This document is distinct from this corpus's existing Post-Offer, Pre-Employment Medical Examination and Pre-Employment and Workplace Drug Testing information sheets: a physical or agility test that measures an applicant's ability to perform actual or simulated job tasks is treated differently under federal regulatory guidance than a medical examination or medical inquiry.

FEHA'S GENERAL PROHIBITION ON HIRING DISCRIMINATION
California's Fair Employment and Housing Act makes it unlawful for an employer, because of an applicant's race, national origin, physical disability, sex, age, or several other listed characteristics, to refuse to hire the person or to discriminate against the person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment. A physical or agility test that Acme, Inc. requires of applicants for Software Engineer is a hiring practice subject to this general prohibition: if the test causes a person to be refused employment because of a listed characteristic, the statute's prohibition is implicated regardless of whether the employer intended to discriminate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For an employer, because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status of any person, to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(a) (California Legislative Information text), California FEHA, general prohibition on employment discrimination because of listed characteristics (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: Government Code section 12940, as fetched and reviewed in full for this document, states this general prohibition and separately addresses medical and psychological examinations and inquiries in subdivisions (e) and (f), but this document's research did not find language in section 12940 itself that spells out a disparate-impact/business-necessity framework in the way 42 U.S.C. section 12112(b)(6) and 42 U.S.C. section 2000e-2(k) do for federal law. This document's research did not verify whether a California regulation (such as a provision of title 2 of the California Code of Regulations) supplies a state-specific codification of that framework for employment tests generally, because the primary free-text source checked for the California Code of Regulations was not accessible during this research session; readers should not assume section 12940's silence on this point means no such state regulation exists. This document is informational only and does not determine whether any specific test or hiring decision violates this statute.

DISABILITY-BASED DISPARATE IMPACT: THE JOB-RELATED, BUSINESS-NECESSITY STANDARD
Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, it is a form of unlawful discrimination for a covered employer to use qualification standards, employment tests, or other selection criteria that screen out or tend to screen out an individual with a disability, or a class of individuals with disabilities, unless the employer shows that the standard, test, or criteria, as used, is job-related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity. The EEOC's implementing regulation restates this same standard for qualification standards, tests, and other selection criteria that screen out on the basis of disability.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "using qualification standards, employment tests or other selection criteria that screen out or tend to screen out an individual with a disability or a class of individuals with disabilities unless the standard, test or other selection criteria, as used by the covered entity, is shown to be job-related for the position in question and is consistent with business necessity"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(6) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, disparate-impact prohibition for qualification standards, tests, and selection criteria (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/12112)
  "It is unlawful for a covered entity to use qualification standards, employment tests or other selection criteria that screen out or tend to screen out an individual with a disability or a class of individuals with disabilities, on the basis of disability, unless the standard, test, or other selection criteria, as used by the covered entity, is shown to be job related for the position in question and is consistent with business necessity."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1630.10(a) (eCFR text), EEOC ADA regulation, qualification standards, tests, and other selection criteria (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1630/section-1630.10)
  Known gap: The statute and its implementing regulation are treated together here as one connected source, since the regulation restates the statutory standard rather than adding an independent one. This provision addresses disparate impact on the basis of disability specifically; it does not by itself address a physical or agility test that has a disparate effect based on sex, age, or another characteristic, which are addressed elsewhere in this document under different statutes. This document is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific physical or agility test screens out individuals with disabilities, and it does not perform or substitute for the job-relatedness or business-necessity showing the law requires an employer to make on the specific facts.

A PHYSICAL AGILITY TEST IS NOT A MEDICAL EXAMINATION
The EEOC's official interpretive guidance to its ADA regulations states that physical agility tests are not medical examinations, and so, unlike a medical examination, may be given at any point in the application or employment process. That guidance also states that such tests must be given to all similarly situated applicants or employees regardless of disability, and that if such a test screens out or tends to screen out an individual with a disability, or a class of individuals with disabilities, the employer would have to demonstrate that the test is job-related and consistent with business necessity and that performance cannot be achieved with reasonable accommodation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Physical agility tests are not medical examinations and so may be given at any point in the application or employment process. Such tests must be given to all similarly situated applicants or employees regardless of disability. If such tests screen out or tend to screen out an individual with a disability or a class of individuals with disabilities, the employer would have to demonstrate that the test is job-related and consistent with business necessity and that performance cannot be achieved with reasonable accommodation."
  — Appendix to 29 C.F.R. Part 1630 (Interpretive Guidance on Title I of the ADA, section on § 1630.14) (eCFR text), EEOC interpretive guidance, physical agility tests distinguished from medical examinations (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1630/appendix-Appendix%20to%20Part%201630)
  Known gap: This quotation comes from the appendix of interpretive guidance to 29 C.F.R. Part 1630, which the EEOC itself describes as guidance rather than a binding regulatory text with independent legal force; it explains the agency's own reading of the regulation rather than adding new statutory or regulatory text. This document's research did not find a parallel statement in California's Government Code section 12940 addressing whether, or at what stage, a physical agility test is distinct from a "medical or psychological examination" for purposes of that section's separate pre-offer and post-offer provisions; whether California law treats physical agility tests the same way this federal guidance does is not resolved by the statutory text this document reviewed. This document is informational only and does not determine whether any specific test is a physical agility test or a medical examination for these purposes.

DISPARATE IMPACT BASED ON SEX OR ANOTHER TITLE VII CHARACTERISTIC
Separately from the ADA's disability-specific framework, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 provides that an unlawful employment practice based on disparate impact is established if a complaining party demonstrates that an employer uses a particular employment practice that causes a disparate impact on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, and the employer fails to demonstrate that the challenged practice is job-related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity. A physical or agility test with a minimum strength, speed, height, or similar performance threshold is a type of employment practice that has historically been analyzed for disparate impact under this statutory framework where it screens out a disproportionate share of applicants of one sex or another protected group.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An unlawful employment practice based on disparate impact is established under this subchapter only if— (i) a complaining party demonstrates that a respondent uses a particular employment practice that causes a disparate impact on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin and the respondent fails to demonstrate that the challenged practice is job related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity;"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(k)(1)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, disparate-impact burden of proof (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000e-2)
  Known gap: This statutory provision codifies a disparate-impact burden-of-proof framework that predates this specific statutory text; a full account of how courts have applied it to physical or agility testing (for example, in cases addressing height, weight, or strength requirements) requires case law that this document's research was not able to independently verify through primary case-law sources within this research session, and no such case is cited here. This document is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific test causes a disparate impact on the basis of sex or another characteristic, and it does not perform or substitute for the statistical showing or the job-relatedness and business-necessity showing the law requires on the specific facts.

FEHA'S PRE-OFFER AND POST-OFFER TIMING RULES FOR MEDICAL OR PSYCHOLOGICAL EXAMINATIONS
Separately from the disparate-impact framework described above, California's FEHA restricts when Acme, Inc. may require a "medical or psychological examination" or make a "medical or psychological inquiry" of Acme, Inc. as a job applicant for Software Engineer. Before a conditional offer, FEHA prohibits requiring such an examination or making such an inquiry, while permitting an inquiry into the applicant's ability to perform job-related functions. After a conditional offer has been made but before employment duties begin, FEHA permits such an examination or inquiry only if it is job-related and consistent with business necessity and all entering employees in the same job classification are subject to the same examination or inquiry.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "for any employer or employment agency to require any medical or psychological examination of an applicant, to make any medical or psychological inquiry of an applicant, to make any inquiry whether an applicant has a mental disability or physical disability or medical condition, or to make any inquiry regarding the nature or severity of a physical disability, mental disability, or medical condition."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California FEHA, pre-offer prohibition on medical or psychological examination and inquiry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "an employer or employment agency may inquire into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions and may respond to an applicant’s request for reasonable accommodation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California FEHA, permitted pre-offer inquiry into job-related functions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  "an employer or employment agency may require a medical or psychological examination or make a medical or psychological inquiry of a job applicant after an employment offer has been made but prior to the commencement of employment duties, provided that the examination or inquiry is job related and consistent with business necessity and that all entering employees in the same job classification are subject to the same examination or inquiry."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California FEHA, permitted post-offer examination or inquiry with job-related/business-necessity requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes FEHA's pre-offer and post-offer provisions for "medical or psychological" examinations and inquiries; whether a given physical or agility test qualifies as a "medical or psychological examination or inquiry" within the meaning of this statute, as opposed to a physical agility test that federal interpretive guidance treats as a non-medical, any-stage test, is not resolved by the statutory text this document reviewed and is not addressed by this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific examination or test, and it does not determine whether a conditional offer has been extended in any given case.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate that you have received and reviewed this information sheet.

Applicant: Acme, Inc.
Position: Software Engineer
Date: September 1, 2026
